items.item: GUI clients section -> http://Git Bash Commonly Used Commands  What is Git? Git is a distributed version control system that controls source code for software development. With Git, it is possible to track code changes efficiently.  What are the advantages of using Git? Before Git, there were several distributed control version systems. However, Git implemented a concept that maintains a copy of the entire local repository, history, changes, and version control.  Git provides features to manage synchronization to repositories that share history. The local copy makes it always available, even without a network connection. The synchronization capability makes it very powerful and flexible.  What is Git Bash? The Bash environment is a Windows command-line terminal. We remark Windows because Git emulates a Unix-style command line. Unix-based operating systems and Mac OS include this type of terminal. Git still provides a Linux/Unix version and macOS as well.  Is Git Bash the only way to use Git? No. Several visual solutions provide Git capabilities, hiding the command's complexity. Many development environments have embedded capabilities or offer the same features as plugins.  The visual solution can include a visual tree representation or just menus with the most common operations. The way operations represent commands is very flexible. Some plugins or environments group more than one command into a single operation. It is essential to understand that most plugins or environments only provide a small set of commands through a visual interface. The Git Bash command line is the only way to access all possible operations.  Installing Git Bash in Windows To install Git Bash in Windows, go to the official page and click the Windows option. https://git-scm.com/downloads The GUI clients section (https://git-scm.com/downloads/guis) also lists the different GUI clients for other platforms. This section groups a comprehensive list of external tools recommended by Git.  Select the default options if you are unsure what options to choose when installing the software.  Configuration commands Configuration commands are generally the first commands to use for new installations. These commands prepare the environment to use Git. For advanced scenarios where developers have multiple accounts for multiple projects, it is possible to use the configuration commands several times at the folder level. Set up your name. This command sets your display name. Remember that this name does not refer to security or login information. git config --global user.name "<Your.full.name>" You can also set up your name for a single repository. To achieve that, you must be inside the project folder in the terminal. Just remove the global option from the command. git config user.name "<Your.full.name>" Set up your email git config --global user.email "<youraddress@domain.com"> Display all configuration options This command is essential to verifying the configuration's correctness. It will display every configuration option. Most are rarely modified, but some are common in enterprise environments. git config --list In some common enterprise scenarios, HTTP and credential store options require modification.  Repository commands Initialize a repository This command initializes a Git repository in the current local folder.  git init Clone an existing repository. This command retrieves a repository from a URL and stores it locally.  git clone <url> Git supports protocols, and URLs might look different depending on the repository. ssh:// git:// http[s]:// ftp[s]:// We recommend visiting the official document for the clone command (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-clone) for more complex scenarios.  Check repository status. The status command displays all changes in the current repository branch.  git status Display branches The display branches command shows a list of branches in the local version of the repository. Suppose anybody updates the server copy after we download the repository. In that case, those branches will not appear in the local version. git branch or git branch --list Switch to another branch. A typical project contains more than one branch. This command switches to another branch. git checkout [another_branch] Delete a branch The delete branch command is uncommon, but if you need it, use the following command. git branch -d [branch_name] This command deletes the local branch. For more advanced cases, such as removing remote branches or eliminating branches with existing changes, we suggest you read the documentation. Commit commands Add files. The add files command lets developers control files to add to a commit. Suppose we modify several files in our project; we can commit all of them at once with the following command: git add . We can specify one file at a time, adding the file name at the end: git add [filename_including_path] Git also supports a list of files separated by commas: git add [filename1],[filename2],[filename3] Git allows the use of wildcards to commit similar files together: git add *.txt Remove files from commit. The RM command removes a file from committing to a repository. This command does not modify the file in any way; it excludes it from the commit to the repository. git rm --cached <filename_including_path> Commit files. When we add files to a commit, Git adds them to the 'staging section.' Once developers are ready to publish them, the commit command indicates that Git should save them in the repository. git commit The most common way to commit is by indicating a message for the changes. For example, let's assume we modified different files to fix a bug; the command will look like this: git commit -m "Bug A fixed" Show differences. The diff command shows the differences between the last commit and the current repository status. git diff Git displays a list of changes, additions, and files removed.   Stash and Pop commands Stash command We train our teams in Git, and one of the most critical functions we know from experience is Stashing and Restoring changes. Git does not allow you to switch branches unless you commit changes.  It is common to have work in progress that you must set aside while conducting other work. Another case to save state is if you have changes in your local environment that you don't want to push to the repository. For example, you add some files for testing purposes or to override a configuration, and you want to preserve those changes before switching to another branch. To stash your current changes, use the following command: git stash After running the command Git, reset the status to the last clean state before any changes and keep those changes in a separate place. To restore the changes to the current branch, use the following command git stash pop If you want to see what is in the stash area, use the command: git stash show You can also delete all the entries in the stash area with the following command: git stash clear Stash command considerations We suggest spending time using stash commands to understand how they work. It is one of the most influential and valuable commands but takes time to master. We observed developers stashing current changes to continue working on the current or another branch. Suppose a developer modifies any files stashed and tries to pop the changes. In that case, the operation leads to conflicts that are not always simple to fix.  Advanced commands Below is a simple list of advanced commands. These operations are complex to learn, and entire articles cover a small portion of each command. Merge command Merge a branch into the current branch. git merge [branch_you_want_to_merge] Erase commits command Reset changes to a specific commit git reset [commit_reference] Reset changes to the HEAD (soft) git reset --soft HEAD^ The reset command is very complex and admits different options to reset the current state to specific commits and heads and even force the elimination of committed files. We recommend reading the documentation and understanding the consequences of forcing resets or reset changes to a particular commit. If you are unsure how it works, this command can cause you to lose essential changes.

fullText:
Services

Custom Development

CUSTOM DEVELOPMENT

Software shaped to the work

When a packaged product bends the workflow out of shape, we design and build the application, the integrations, and the internal tools around the way the company already operates.

Talk through the workflow

What we build

Custom development at OLIANT is the software between the systems you already run: the application people use, the APIs that connect it, and the jobs that keep the data moving.

Business applications

We build the application staff, customers, or partners open to complete a job: a case workspace, an operations console, a portal, or a back office that a spreadsheet can no longer carry.

The interface, the rules, and the permissions follow the workflow. A screen exists because someone has to finish a step, not because a template included it.

Integrations and APIs

Most custom systems have to read and write something that already exists: a database, an ERP, a payment provider, or a file that arrives on a schedule. We put that exchange behind an API with a contract the other side can rely on.

Where a product already has an integration point, we use it. Where it does not, we add a narrow service instead of copying data into a second source of truth.

Internal tools

Some of the most useful software never faces a customer. We build the tools a team uses to review exceptions, approve a step, or correct a record without asking an engineer to run a query.

Those tools stay small. They call the same services as the main application, so a fix in the tool is a fix in the system.

A stack we already practice

The language follows the problem and the team that will own the code. We build on Java, Node, Python, .NET, and React, and we say which one we recommend before the project starts.

Public sites and content-managed pages stay with web development when that is the better fit. Custom development is for the application behavior a theme or a site builder does not express.

Typical use cases

These are the situations where a custom build is the straightforward option. They are project shapes, not stories about a particular client.

A workflow that outgrew the spreadsheet

Several people edit the same tracker, versions drift, and nobody can tell which row is current. We replace that tracker with an application that keeps one record, a history, and a permission for each role.

A portal in front of an existing system

Customers or partners need a simpler view of a system they should not log into directly. We build the portal and the API in front of that system, and we leave the system of record where it is.

Two products that have to act as one

An order, a ticket, or a policy lives in more than one product. We build the integration and the screen that shows the combined state, including what happens when one side is down.

A product that no longer matches the process

The current tool can stay for the parts it still does well. We replace the part that fights the process, and we connect the new piece back so people are not retyping the same facts.

How we work

The engagement follows the workflow, then the software. Scope is a slice a person can complete, not a diagram of every screen the product might grow into.

Name the job the software has to finish

We start from the steps a person takes, the data those steps need, and the systems that already hold that data. The first written result is that path, plus what is explicitly out of the first release.

Choose the stack in the open

We recommend a language and a framework from the ones we practice, and we explain the choice against the team that will maintain the code. A new stack is not introduced for its own sake.

Build the slice and the integration together

The first release includes the screen and the connection it depends on. A demo that only works against fake data is not the milestone. The milestone is a user finishing the step against the real system, or against a faithful test double we can replace.

Test, release, and leave the code with you

QA sits in the same delivery. We use the practices on our QA page: checks that match the risk, run before the release, and stay in the repository. If you would rather extend an internal team than hand over a whole build, staff augmentation is the other shape.

Bring the workflow, not a feature list

Tell us the job the software has to finish and the systems it has to touch. We will say what belongs in a first release.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

Custom development here is one team across the application, the integration, and the checks that have to pass before release.

The boundary is part of the design

We write down what the new software owns and what stays in the systems you already have. That boundary is how the project stays smaller than a rewrite.

QA is in the same delivery

Testing is not a separate vendor at the end. The checks live with the code and run against the workflow the release is supposed to support.

You keep the codebase

The repository, the pipeline, and the notes on how to run the project stay with you. A later change does not depend on a hidden environment.

Frequently asked questions

Questions we expect before a custom build starts.

When is custom software the wrong choice?

When a product you can configure already matches the workflow, including its awkward parts. We will say so. Custom development is for the gap a configuration screen cannot close, not for rebuilding a commodity tool.

Do we have to replace the system we already use?

No. A common shape is a new application or portal in front of the current system, with an API between them. Replacement is a later decision, made after the new path is in use.

Who owns the code when the project is done?

You do. The work lands in your repository, with the build and the tests. We can stay to extend it, or your team can take the next change.

Can you work beside our developers?

Yes. Some projects are a full build. Others add people to a team you already have, through staff augmentation, with the same stack and the same review habits.

How do you choose the language?

From the problem and from the people who will maintain the code. Java, Node, Python, .NET, and React are the stacks we practice. The recommendation is part of the first conversation, before build effort starts.

Start from the job to be done

Describe the workflow and the systems around it. We will tell you what we would build first, and what we would leave alone.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

Java

JAVA DEVELOPMENT

JVM systems that stay maintainable

We design, extend, and maintain Java services: Spring Boot for newer APIs, Jakarta EE where the application already lives there, and the batch and integration jobs that sit beside both.

Review your Java stack

What we build with Java

Java work here is server-side. We use the JVM, a build you can reproduce, and a module boundary that a later change can find.

Spring Boot services

New HTTP services are usually Spring Boot: controllers or functional routes, Spring Security where the API needs an identity, and Spring Data or jOOQ against the database you already have. Dependencies stay in Maven or Gradle, pinned, with a build that fails when the lockfile drifts.

We keep the service bootable from a main class and from a container. Configuration comes from the environment, not from a file that only exists on one laptop.

Jakarta EE and existing JVM applications

Plenty of Java worth keeping is not a new Spring service. We work in Jakarta EE and in the older Java EE layouts still running in application servers: servlets, CDI, JPA, and the deployment descriptor the server actually reads.

A change in that codebase starts by reading the modules that already exist. We do not open a rewrite because a newer framework is more familiar.

APIs, messaging, and batch

Services expose REST with an explicit contract. Where the system already uses a queue, we add producers and consumers on that broker, JMS or Kafka, instead of inventing a second channel.

Scheduled work stays in its own entry point: Spring Batch, a Quartz job, or the scheduler the current application uses. A batch failure is visible as a failed job, not as a request that timed out.

Tests that follow the module

JUnit covers the domain rules. An API change also gets a test that boots the slice and calls the endpoint. Testcontainers is the default when the test needs a real database or broker, so the suite is not asserting against a mock that hides a SQL mistake.

Typical use cases

Java is the right tool when the system is already on the JVM, or when the service has to live for years beside a relational database and a set of internal callers.

An internal API in front of a relational database

Several applications need the same customer, policy, or inventory rules. We put those rules in a Java service with a documented API, and we stop copying the SQL into each caller.

A module added to a monolith

The current WAR or Spring application can take a new package with a clear boundary. We add the module, its schema changes, and its tests, and we leave the unrelated packages alone.

A nightly or hourly job

Files arrive, records need reconciling, or a downstream system wants a feed. We build that job on the JVM, with a rerun story for the rows that failed, rather than hiding it inside a web request.

A service that has to meet an existing security model

The company already has an identity provider and a set of roles. We map those into Spring Security or the application server's constraints, and we test the paths that must stay forbidden.

How we work

Java engagements start in the repository you have. The first week is for the build, the runtime, and the boundary of the change.

Read the build before writing features

We identify the JDK version, Maven or Gradle, the application server if there is one, and the tests that already run. A feature that does not build the way the team builds is not done.

Agree the package boundary

New code goes in a package or module with a public API small enough to name. Callers inside the same repository use that API. Reaching into another module's internals is a review comment, not a shortcut.

Prove the endpoint and the job

Unit tests cover the rules. A running slice covers the HTTP contract or the batch step, including the failure we expect when a dependency is down. We do not treat a green unit suite as proof the service starts.

Release beside the current deployment

The artifact is the one your pipeline already knows, or a container if that is how this service is deployed. We add the health check and the log fields operators use, and we roll out next to the version that is live.

Bring the repository, including the old parts

Spring Boot, Jakarta EE, or a mix of both. We will tell you what we would change first and what we would leave on the current JDK.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

Java at OLIANT includes the application you already run, not only a greenfield Spring service.

Old and new Java in one review

We read application-server layouts and Spring Boot services with the same care. The recommendation follows the code that is in production.

The JVM stays operable

Memory, startup, and dependency updates are part of the change. A service that only works with a hand-tuned laptop JDK is not finished.

A boundary you can point at

Packages, public types, and tests mark what the change owns. The next developer can find the edge without an oral history.

Frequently asked questions

Practical questions about Java work, before a project starts.

Do you only take Spring Boot?

No. Spring Boot is the usual choice for a new service. Jakarta EE and existing application-server code are in scope when that is what production runs. We will not propose a framework migration as the price of a small feature.

Which JDK versions do you work with?

The version the application already builds on, and a current LTS when we are starting a new service. Moving an old service to a newer JDK is its own piece of work, with the test suite as the gate, not a side effect of an unrelated feature.

Can you add an API without rewriting the monolith?

Yes. That is a common shape: a new package or a new Spring service that owns one area, with the monolith calling it or being called by it. The data ownership is decided before the first endpoint is published.

How do you handle database access?

With the approach already in the codebase when there is one: JPA, jOOQ, JDBC, or Spring Data. A new service gets one of those, chosen for the queries it has to run, and the schema change ships with the code that uses it.

Where does Java sit next to our other systems?

Java is the service and the job. React or another front end calls it. Cloud hosting, including Microsoft Azure when the company already runs there, is a separate decision from the language. Custom development is the page for the wider product shape around that service.

Keep the JVM application you have

Tell us the JDK, the framework, and the change you need. We will work inside that build.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

Node

NODE DEVELOPMENT

APIs and services on Node.js

We build Node.js services in TypeScript: HTTP APIs, backends for a specific front end, and workers that share the same language without blocking the request path.

Plan the Node service

What we build with Node

Node is the runtime. The framework, the types, and the process model are chosen so the event loop stays available and the API stays describable.

HTTP APIs in TypeScript

Express is the default when the service is a thin HTTP layer. NestJS fits when the team wants modules, dependency injection, and a structure that several services can share. Fastify fits when the service is performance-sensitive and the plugin model is enough.

Request and response bodies are typed. A route that accepts an untyped object and hopes the front end sends the right shape does not pass review.

A backend for a specific client

Web and mobile clients often need an API shaped for one screen, not a mirror of every downstream system. We build that backend-for-frontend in Node, and we keep the aggregation here so the client is not calling five services on each view. React applications are a common caller.

The BFF owns caching headers, auth token handling for that client, and the error shape the UI can show. It does not become a second copy of the domain rules.

Workers off the request path

Email, file processing, and webhook fan-out do not belong inside the request that triggered them. We put that work on a queue, BullMQ or the broker you already run, and a separate Node process consumes it.

The HTTP process stays short. The worker can retry, fail, and be restarted without taking the API down with it.

Runtime, packages, and logs

We pin the Node version in the engine field and in the environment that runs it. npm or pnpm is chosen once, and the lockfile is part of the build. Native addons are a decision, not an accident from a transitive dependency.

Logs are structured. A health endpoint reports whether the process can reach the dependencies it needs. The host, whether a container, a platform service, or a VM, restarts from that signal.

Typical use cases

Node fits JavaScript teams and services whose main job is HTTP, aggregation, or a stream of events.

An API the product UI calls

The screen needs a single payload. We build the Node API that assembles it, validates the write, and returns an error the interface can put next to a field.

Webhooks and third-party callbacks

A provider posts an event and expects a fast acknowledgement. The Node route verifies the signature, stores the event, and lets a worker do the slow part.

A real-time feature next to the API

When the product needs a live update, we add WebSockets or Server-Sent Events on the same TypeScript codebase, with an explicit story for reconnect and for what the client should do when the socket drops.

A service in front of an older system

The system of record stays where it is. Node translates its API, its files, or its database into the contract the new client expects, and it isolates timeouts so a slow downstream call does not stall every request.

How we work

A Node project is a runtime choice, a framework choice, and a test that hits the HTTP stack. We settle those before the endpoint list grows.

Pin the runtime and the package manager

The Node version, the package manager, and the TypeScript config are fixed in the repo. CI uses the same ones. A feature branch that only runs on a newer Node than production is not ready.

Pick one framework and say why

Express, NestJS, or Fastify. The reason is written down: team familiarity, module structure, or measured need for the faster server. We do not mix three HTTP frameworks in one service.

Test the route, not only the function

Vitest or Jest covers units. Supertest, or the framework's own test client, calls the route with the headers and the body a real client would send, including the cases the schema should reject.

Split the process from the work it queues

If the service accepts work that outlives the request, that work has its own process and its own health check. Deploying the API does not silently drop the jobs, and deploying the worker does not restart every open connection by accident.

Tell us who calls the API

A browser, a mobile app, another service, or a webhook. The caller decides the shape of the Node service more than the framework does.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

Node at OLIANT is TypeScript, a single HTTP stack, and a process model that keeps slow work off the event loop.

Types on the contract

The payload the client sends and the payload it receives are typed and validated. Drift shows up in review, not in a production log.

One framework per service

Express, NestJS, or Fastify, chosen for a reason. The next endpoint follows that choice instead of introducing a second style.

The event loop stays free

Long work moves to a worker. The API process answers, logs, and shuts down cleanly when the host asks it to.

Frequently asked questions

Questions that come up when a team is deciding on Node.

Do you write Node in plain JavaScript?

New services are TypeScript. We will work in an existing JavaScript codebase, and we add types at the boundary we touch rather than pausing the project for a whole-repo conversion.

Which framework should we use?

Express when you want the least framework. NestJS when several modules and a shared structure matter. Fastify when you want a schema-first server and you have measured a need for it. We pick one for the service and keep it.

Is Node a fit for CPU-heavy work?

Usually no. Node is for IO: HTTP, queues, files, and upstream APIs. Heavy computation belongs in a worker, another process, or another language. We will say so if the workload is a mismatch.

Can the same team build the React UI?

Yes, when the project includes the front end. React is a separate practice with its own page. The Node service still has its own contract, so the UI and the API can release on different days.

How do you deploy it?

On the platform you already use: a container, a process manager, or a cloud service that runs Node. The repository contains the start command, the health check, and the Node version. The host is allowed to kill the process and start it again.

A Node service with a contract

Bring the caller and the downstream systems. We will propose the framework, the process split, and the first endpoints.

Let's get in touch

fullText:
Services

Development

Python

PYTHON DEVELOPMENT

Services and jobs in Python

We build Python web services and the scripts that move data around them. Django when the product needs an application and an admin. FastAPI or Flask when it needs a smaller HTTP API. A separate entry point when the work is a job, not a request.

Talk through the Python work

What we build with Python

Python is readable, and that is only an advantage if the project has one way to run, one way to install, and a clear split between the web process and the jobs.

Django applications

Django fits an application with models, an admin, and server-rendered or API views. We use Django REST framework when the same models need a JSON API, and we keep business rules on the model or a service module rather than in the view.

Migrations ship with the code that depends on them. The admin is configured for the people who will use it, including which fields they must not edit.

FastAPI and Flask APIs

FastAPI is the usual choice for a typed HTTP API: Pydantic models on the boundary, dependency injection for the database session, and OpenAPI generated from those types. Flask remains a good fit for a small service or for an application that already uses it.

We do not grow a Flask app into an informal Django. If the project needs an admin, auth, and a migration story, we start with Django or we add those pieces on purpose.

Jobs and automation

A report, a file ingest, or a sync with another system gets its own module and its own command. Celery, RQ, or a scheduled container runs it. The web worker does not import a script that takes minutes.

pandas is available when the job is tabular. It is not the application framework. Data frames stay inside the job that needs them.

Environments and tests

Dependencies are locked, with uv, pip-tools, or Poetry, and the choice is written down. The same lock installs in CI and in the image that runs production. pytest covers the service and the job, including the database the ORM or the SQL actually hits.

Typical use cases

Python earns its place when the team wants one language for the HTTP service and for the automation around it, without pretending those are the same process.

An internal tool with an admin

A team needs to review records, correct a field, and export a slice. Django gives them that admin and a permission model. We build the models around the review step, not around every column in the source system.

A small API next to a data store

One or two resources, a clear schema, and a few callers. FastAPI or Flask is enough. We publish the schema and the error format, and we stop before the service accumulates unused apps.

A file or report that someone runs by hand

A workbook arrives, a person cleans it, and a system of record is updated. We turn that into a Python job with validation, a reject file, and a way to rerun the failed rows.

A glue service between two APIs

Python is a direct way to translate one provider's payload into another's. We keep the translation in a tested module, with timeouts and a record of what was sent, rather than in a notebook that only one person can run.

How we work

Python projects fail quietly when the environment is tribal knowledge. We make the install, the framework, and the job boundary boring on purpose.

Lock the interpreter and the dependencies

The Python version is the one production runs. The lockfile is the install. A developer machine that needs extra undocumented packages is a bug in the repo, and we fix it before adding features.

Choose Django, FastAPI, or Flask once

The framework matches the product: Django for an application with an admin, FastAPI for a typed API, Flask for a small existing or narrow service. Mixing them inside one deployable is not a phase we plan for.

Keep jobs out of the web process

Anything that waits on a file, a large query, or another company's API is a command or a queue task. The web process validates, records the request, and returns. The job reports success or a specific failure.

Test the boundary that can break

pytest, with the database and the HTTP client the code uses. A typed schema is checked against an example payload. A job is tested with the bad file we expect, not only the happy path.

Say whether this is a service or a job

Django, FastAPI, Flask, or a scheduled script. The shape of the work matters more than a preference for the language.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

Python at OLIANT keeps the web service and the data job in the same language and in different processes.

One framework, named up front

Django, FastAPI, or Flask is a project decision with a reason. Later features follow it.

Jobs are first-class

Ingest, sync, and reports have a command, a failure mode, and a test. They are not hidden inside a view.

The environment is in the repo

Interpreter version and locked dependencies install the same way in CI and in production. Setup is a command, not a checklist in chat.

Frequently asked questions

Questions we answer before choosing a Python stack.

Should we use Django or FastAPI?

Django when you need models, an admin, and the batteries that come with a full application. FastAPI when you are publishing a typed HTTP API and you do not need that admin. Flask when the service is small or already written in Flask. We pick one.

Do you build data-science models?

We build the Python services and jobs around data: APIs, ingest, validation, and the code that puts rows where the application can read them. Training and evaluating a machine-learning model is a different engagement, and we will not describe a data job as if it were one.

How do you package Python for production?

A locked install in a container or a host virtual environment, with the web server named: gunicorn or uvicorn, depending on the framework. The start command, the worker count, and the health check are part of the repository.

Can Python call the rest of our stack?

Yes. A Python service can sit beside Java, Node, or .NET systems and talk to them over HTTP or a queue. Custom development is the wider page when the Python piece is one part of a product.

Python with a way to run it

Tell us whether you need an application, an API, or a job. We will name the framework and the process split.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

WebFlow

WEBFLOW DEVELOPMENT

Sites editors can change

We design and build in Webflow: marketing and content sites whose pages, CMS collections, and interactions a non-developer can update, with custom code limited to the spots the Designer cannot cover.

Plan the Webflow site

What we build with Webflow

Webflow is a visual builder with a real CMS and a publish model. The work is the content structure and the class system, not a screenshot turned into a single long page.

Marketing and campaign sites

Landing pages, product marketing, and campaign sections are built in the Designer against your brand styles. Components and classes are named so a second page reuses them instead of duplicating a pile of overrides.

Interactions stay purposeful: a state change a visitor can follow, not a chain of timelines nobody can edit later.

CMS collections

Articles, locations, people, or project pages become collections with fields an editor understands. Reference fields connect related items. The template is built once and bound to those fields, including the empty state.

We decide which pages are static and which are CMS items before visual polish, so a new entry does not require a designer.

Forms, embeds, and the edge of the Designer

Native Webflow forms cover the common lead and contact flows. When a form has to talk to a system Webflow does not know, we add a custom embed or a small script and we document what it sends.

Memberships, localization, and ecommerce are used when the project needs them. They are project settings with an editorial consequence, so we set them up with the person who will publish, not only in a preview link.

Publishing and performance

Assets are sized for the layout. Fonts and third-party scripts are listed. We check the published site, not only the Designer canvas, including the CMS template at a phone width.

A Webflow site can sit next to a web development property. We say which URLs belong in Webflow and which belong in an application.

Typical use cases

Webflow is a strong fit when marketers and editors need to publish without a deploy, and the site does not have to behave like a product application.

A company site with a few templates

Home, a handful of product pages, and a CMS for news or resources. Editors add items. Designers change a component. Engineers are not in the loop for a headline.

Campaign pages on a shared style

A launch needs a page this week and another next month. We build the sections as reusable components so the next campaign is an assembly, not a new file.

A content collection with relationships

Authors, categories, and articles, or offices and regions. The collection fields match the way the team files the content, including the fields that are required before publish.

A visual site that still needs one custom behavior

A calculator, a gated asset, or a script from another product. We embed that piece and keep the rest of the page in Webflow, so the custom code has an edge.

How we work

Webflow projects are won or lost in the CMS and the class names. Visual design follows that structure.

Model the collections first

We list the item types, the fields, and who is allowed to edit them. Static pages are named separately. A field that only exists to force a layout is removed before build.

Build components, then pages

Classes and components land before the long pages. A new section reuses them. Overrides are the exception, and they are named so the next editor can see them.

Add custom code in a marked place

Embeds and site-level scripts are written down: what they do, which page they load on, and what breaks if they are removed. The Designer remains the place editors work.

Hand over the Editor

We walk through publishing, CMS items, and the components editors may change. The preview link is not the handover. The handover is an editor publishing a real item.

Bring the pages and who will edit them

We will map those pages onto static layouts and CMS collections, and we will mark anything that needs custom code.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

Webflow at OLIANT is a site an editor can publish, with custom code kept at the edge.

Collections before decoration

Fields and templates are decided first. A new CMS item fills a page that was built for it.

Classes a second person can read

Components and class names stay consistent, so the next campaign does not fork the design system by accident.

Custom code is listed

Every embed has a reason and a page. Editors are not left to discover a script by breaking a layout.

Frequently asked questions

Questions to settle before a Webflow build.

Is Webflow the same as WordPress?

No. Both let editors publish, and the editing models differ. Webflow designs and content live in Webflow's hosting and CMS. WordPress is PHP, themes, and plugins on a host you control. We use each where it fits, and we do not rebuild one inside the other.

Can our team edit the site after launch?

Yes. That is the point of the Editor and the CMS. We set roles, required fields, and components so an editor can publish an item or change a section without opening the full Designer.

What happens when we need logic Webflow does not have?

We add a bounded embed or connect the form to another system, and we write down the dependency. If the site is becoming an application, with accounts, complex state, and its own data rules, we move that part to custom development instead of stretching the Designer.

Do you migrate an existing site into Webflow?

We can rebuild the pages and import content into collections when the content maps cleanly onto fields. A pixel-by-pixel copy of a site that depends on a custom application is a different project, and we will separate the marketing pages from the application URLs.

A Webflow site with an editor in mind

Share the page list and who will publish. We will come back with the collections, the components, and the custom code we would avoid.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

WordPress

WORDPRESS DEVELOPMENT

WordPress that stays updatable

We build and maintain WordPress sites on the block editor: a theme that holds the design, plugins that hold custom behavior, and an update path that is tried on staging before it touches production.

Review the WordPress site

What we build with WordPress

WordPress is PHP, a database, and a plugin ecosystem. We keep custom code in the places core updates will not erase.

Block themes and the Site Editor

New sites use a block theme. Templates and template parts express the layout. theme.json carries the type, color, and spacing so editors stay inside the design instead of pasting inline styles.

A classic PHP theme stays when the site already depends on it. We extend it with a child theme. We do not edit a parent theme that the next update will overwrite.

Blocks and patterns

Repeated sections become block patterns or a small custom block. Editors insert the pattern. They do not rebuild a hero from twenty loose blocks every time.

A custom block is registered from a plugin, with the attributes it needs and a fallback in the editor. The theme does not secretly own behavior the content depends on.

Plugins, including WooCommerce

We prefer a maintained plugin when it matches the need. A custom plugin is for the behavior that should survive a theme change: a content type, an integration, a checkout rule.

WooCommerce is in scope for catalogs, checkout, and the hooks a store actually needs. Product data and payment settings stay in WooCommerce. Presentation stays in the theme. Broader storefront engineering also sits with web development.

Updates, staging, and headless when it is real

Core, theme, and plugin updates land on a staging copy first. We check the editor and the public templates, then production. A site with no staging is the first thing we add.

Headless WordPress, with the REST API feeding a separate front end such as React, is a choice we make when the editorial team wants WordPress and the interface cannot be a theme. It is not the default.

Typical use cases

WordPress fits content sites and stores whose editors live in wp-admin and whose hosting you can update.

A company site on the block editor

Pages, posts, and a small set of patterns. Marketing can publish. The theme stops them from inventing a new layout on every page, without closing the editor.

A catalog on WooCommerce

Products, variations, and checkout through WooCommerce. Custom work is the piece the store needs that a setting does not cover, written as a plugin with a test on staging.

A site drowning in plugins

We list what each plugin does, remove the ones that overlap, and replace a fragile combination with one custom plugin when that is smaller than the pile.

Editorial WordPress with a separate front end

Authors stay in WordPress. The public site is an application that reads the REST API. We version the fields the front end depends on, so an editor change does not silently break a route.

How we work

WordPress maintenance is part of the build. A theme that cannot take an update is unfinished.

Separate theme, plugin, and content

Design tokens and templates live in the theme. Behavior the content needs lives in a plugin. Posts and pages live in the database, exported when we need a copy. We do not hide PHP in a widget body.

Stage every update

Staging is a copy of production with the same PHP version and the same active plugins. Updates are applied there, the editor and the public pages are checked, and only then does production change.

Name the load-bearing plugins

The handover lists which plugins can be removed and which ones the theme or the content assumes. WooCommerce, a forms plugin, or an SEO plugin is called out with the version we tested.

Leave wp-admin usable

Roles match the people who will log in. Patterns are available in the inserter. A custom block has a name an editor recognizes. We watch someone publish a page before we call the work done.

Tell us the theme, the plugins, and the PHP version

An existing site or a new one. We will say what belongs in a theme, what belongs in a plugin, and what should be removed.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

WordPress at OLIANT is a site you can update, with custom behavior in a plugin and design in the theme.

Updates are rehearsed

Staging sees the core and plugin updates first. Production is the second step, not the experiment.

Custom code has an address

Plugins hold behavior. Child themes or block themes hold design. Content is not the place we store PHP.

The editor is part of the test

A page that looks right when we build it and breaks when an editor touches it is not finished. Publishing is part of the check.

Frequently asked questions

Questions about how we take on WordPress work.

Will you work on an old classic theme?

Yes. We use a child theme and we avoid a rewrite unless the parent theme is blocking an update you need. A block theme is the recommendation for a new site, not a surprise migration in the middle of a content change.

How do you decide between a plugin and custom code?

A maintained plugin wins when it does the job and its update history is acceptable. Custom code wins when the behavior is specific to your content model or when several plugins are doing the same thing badly. The custom code is a plugin either way.

Can you build a WooCommerce store?

Yes. Products, checkout, and the custom rules that settings cannot express. Payment provider configuration stays in WooCommerce. We test the purchase path on staging, including the email and the stock change.

Is headless WordPress worth it?

When editors want WordPress and the public experience cannot be a theme. It adds a second application, a React front end or another client, and a contract for the fields. For a marketing site, a theme is the smaller system, and we will recommend it.

Who applies security updates?

Whoever we agree will own the staging check. We can do that as part of the engagement: review the update on staging, confirm the editor and the templates, then apply it. We do not leave core updates as an unnamed task.

WordPress you can update next month

Share the theme, the plugin list, and the PHP version. We will tell you what we would keep.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

Google Cloud Platform

GOOGLE CLOUD PLATFORM

Run the workload on Google Cloud

We design how an application runs on Google Cloud Platform: the project and IAM layout, the runtime that fits the process, and the data services it is allowed to use. OLIANT is listed as a Google Cloud Partner in our services menu. This page is that platform work.

Map the GCP project

What we build on Google Cloud Platform

The platform choice follows the process. A request-sized container, a Kubernetes cluster, and a virtual machine are different operating models, and we pick one.

Projects, folders, and IAM

Each environment gets a project. Folders group those projects when the organization needs it. Service accounts own deploy and runtime access. Human users do not share a key.

IAM bindings are written down: who can deploy, who can read production data, and which APIs are enabled. A new service starts from that list.

Cloud Run, GKE, and Compute Engine

Cloud Run is the default for a stateless container with HTTP or a job. GKE is for a workload that already needs Kubernetes: several services, a mesh, or a platform team that will run the cluster. Compute Engine is for the process that has to be a VM.

We do not put a single container on GKE to make the diagram look complete. The runtime matches who will operate it.

Data services the application is allowed to touch

Cloud SQL for relational data the application queries. Cloud Storage for objects and uploads. BigQuery when the work is analysis over large tables, not a row the user is editing. Memorystore when a cache is actually required.

Pub/Sub carries events between services. A service publishes a message it can name. Consumers are separate deploys with their own service accounts.

Build and release

Cloud Build, or the pipeline you already run, builds the artifact and deploys it into the right project. Environments are not two folders in the same project with a comment that says prod.

Logs and error reporting are on from the first deploy. A service without a way to tell a failed revision from a healthy one is not ready for traffic.

Typical use cases

These are the platform shapes we set up. They are not a claim about a particular customer's bill or traffic.

A container service on Cloud Run

An API or a worker with a container, a concurrency setting, and a service account that can reach Cloud SQL or Cloud Storage. Revisions are the rollback.

A cluster that already has a reason

GKE when several services share a cluster and someone will own node pools, upgrades, and namespaces. We set the namespace, the workload identity, and the deploy. We do not treat the cluster as a substitute for IAM.

Analysis that should not hit the application database

Events or exports land in BigQuery. The application database stays for transactions. Queries for reporting run against BigQuery, with a dataset and a group that is allowed to read it.

An existing application moving onto GCP

We start with what the process needs: a VM, a container, or a managed SQL instance. The move is a runtime and a data store, plus the IAM that replaces the old shared login.

How we work

Google Cloud work starts with identity and projects. Product selection comes after we know who deploys and where data lives.

Draw the projects and the accounts

Development, staging, and production are separate projects unless there is a written reason not to. Service accounts are created for deploy and for runtime. Keys are a last resort.

Match the runtime to the process

HTTP container, Kubernetes workload, scheduled job, or VM. We name the Google Cloud product and the operational task it creates, including who upgrades it.

Put data in the service that fits the question

Transactions in Cloud SQL. Objects in Cloud Storage. Analytical queries in BigQuery. The application gets credentials for the one it needs, not for the whole project.

Deploy from a pipeline into that project

The pipeline identity can deploy to the target project and cannot rummage through another environment. A rollback is a previous revision or a previous image, tried before the production project depends on it.

Start with the project layout

Tell us what runs today and who is allowed to deploy. We will place it on Cloud Run, GKE, or Compute Engine with IAM to match.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

Google Cloud Platform at OLIANT is the project, the identity, and the runtime. The Google Cloud Partner listing in our menu points at this work.

IAM before the product icon

Projects and service accounts are the first deliverable. A runtime is added only after we know who can deploy it.

One runtime, with an operator

Cloud Run, GKE, or Compute Engine is chosen with the person who will upgrade it. The diagram and the on-call task match.

Data access is specific

Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage, and BigQuery are granted per service account. Reporting does not log into the transaction database.

Frequently asked questions

Questions about how we use Google Cloud Platform.

What does the Google Cloud Partner listing mean here?

OLIANT is listed as a Google Cloud Partner in the services menu. On this page that means we design and run workloads on Google Cloud Platform: projects, IAM, and the managed services the application uses.

Should we use Cloud Run or GKE?

Cloud Run when you have a container and you want revisions, scale, and a small operating surface. GKE when you already need Kubernetes and someone will run the cluster. A single service is rarely a reason to start a cluster.

Can you work in an organization that already has folders and policies?

Yes. We use the folder, project, and organization policies you have. New services get projects and service accounts inside that structure. We do not stand up a shadow organization beside it.

Do you also build on AWS or Azure?

Yes. AWS and Microsoft Azure have their own pages. A system can span more than one cloud, and we still keep each environment's identity and data access explicit. The application language is a separate choice, covered under custom development.

A Google Cloud layout you can explain

Bring the current hosting and the people who deploy. We will propose the projects, the runtime, and the data services.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

AWS

AWS DEVELOPMENT

The AWS services the workload needs

We place an application on AWS by the way the work runs: Lambda for short requests, ECS or EKS for containers that stay up, and a written boundary for accounts, IAM, S3, and RDS.

Sketch the AWS layout

What we build on AWS

AWS has many services. A project uses the small set that matches the workload, described in code so the next environment is not a click-through.

Accounts and IAM

Environments are separate accounts when the organization can support that, and separate IAM boundaries inside an account when it cannot. Roles are assumed. Long-lived access keys are not how a person logs in, and they are not how a service authenticates if a role will do.

The pipeline role can deploy what it owns. It cannot read another environment because the names happen to match.

Lambda, ECS, and EKS

Lambda fits a request or an event that finishes quickly and can tolerate a cold start. ECS fits a container you want running, on Fargate or on instances you already operate. EKS fits a team that has chosen Kubernetes and will run the cluster.

API Gateway or an application load balancer is the front door when the service needs one. CloudFront sits in front of public static assets and, when it helps, in front of the HTTP entry.

S3, RDS, and queues

S3 holds objects, with a bucket policy and a lifecycle for the data that should expire. RDS holds relational data, in the engine the application already speaks, in a private subnet. SQS or SNS carries work that must outlive the request.

The application receives permission for its bucket and its database. A wildcard on the account is a defect.

Infrastructure in code

CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or Terraform describes the stack. The format is the one the team will edit. A console change that is not imported back into that description does not count as done.

Logs go to CloudWatch with a retention. Alarms cover the failure you would page on, not every metric the service happens to emit.

Typical use cases

The right AWS shape depends on how long the work runs and who will operate it.

An event or HTTP handler on Lambda

A webhook, a file arriving in S3, or a short API method. The function has a timeout, a role, and a test that invokes it with the event it will really receive.

A container service on ECS

An API that stays up, with a task definition, a target group, and a deploy that replaces tasks. Fargate when you do not want to patch instances. EC2-backed ECS when you already run the hosts.

Kubernetes that is a deliberate choice

EKS for a platform team with more than one service and a reason to share a cluster. Namespaces and IAM roles for service accounts are part of the first deploy, not a later cleanup.

A public site with private data

CloudFront and S3 for the public assets. The API and RDS stay in private subnets. The browser never receives a path to the database, and the bucket is not the application log store.

How we work

We name the account boundary and the compute model before we add services. Extra AWS products have to pay for their operational cost.

Fix the account and the network

Which account, which VPC, which subnets are public. The application's security groups are written to the destinations it calls. A wide-open security group is not a temporary step we leave in the template.

Choose Lambda, ECS, or EKS for a reason

The reason is duration, deploy style, and who patches the platform. We record it next to the template. A second compute model inside the same service needs its own justification.

Describe it in the tool you will keep

CDK, CloudFormation, or Terraform. One of them. Parameters cover the differences between environments. Secrets live in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, referenced by the task, not pasted into a task definition.

Rehearse the deploy and the rollback

Staging is another account or another isolated stack, built from the same template. We deploy there, check the health endpoint, and roll back once so production is not the first time the rollback path runs.

Bring the runtime you have in mind

Lambda, a container, or a cluster. We will match it to an account layout, a data store, and a template you can apply again.

Schedule a call

Why OLIANT

AWS at OLIANT is a short list of services, an IAM boundary, and a template that can rebuild the environment.

Compute follows the work

Lambda, ECS, or EKS is a decision about duration and operations. It is written down with the template.

Accounts mean environments

Identity and network boundaries separate staging from production. A shared admin key is not the deployment plan.

The console is not the source

CDK, CloudFormation, or Terraform holds the stack. A click in the console is either imported or reverted.

Frequently asked questions

Questions we answer before choosing AWS services.

Do you default to serverless?

No. Lambda is the right tool for short, event-driven work. A service that stays warm, holds a connection pool, or takes a long time belongs on ECS or another container runtime. We choose after looking at the work.

Can you work in our existing organization?

Yes. We use your AWS Organizations structure, your VPCs, and your pipeline. New stacks land in the account you designate, with roles that fit the permission model you already enforce.

Which infrastructure tool do you use?

The one your team will edit. CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or Terraform. We do not introduce a second tool beside a stack you already maintain.

How does this relate to Google Cloud or Azure?

They are separate pages because the identity model and the product names differ. We can run a piece of a system on AWS and another piece elsewhere, with an explicit contract between them. The application itself is described under custom development and the language pages.

An AWS stack you can apply twice

Tell us the workload and the account you have. We will name the compute, the data services, and the template.

Let's get in touch

Services

Development

Microsoft Azure

MICROSOFT AZURE

Azure for the stack you run

We run applications on Microsoft Azure the way a Microsoft-centered team already works: resource groups per environment, Entra ID for access, and App Service, Functions, or AKS chosen for the process.

Lay out the Azure subscription

What we build on Microsoft Azure

Azure work lines up with identity and with the runtime. .NET is a frequent application stack here. The platform decisions are still about resource groups, access, and how the process runs.

Subscriptions, resource groups, and Entra ID

Environments are resource groups with a naming scheme, or separate subscriptions when the organization already splits that way. Entra ID groups decide who can deploy and who can read production.

Managed identities call Azure SQL, Storage, or Service Bus. A connection string in an app setting is the fallback, stored as a secret, not as a value in the repository.

App Service, Functions, and AKS

App Service hosts the site or API that should stay up, including the .NET applications OLIANT has long built. Deployment slots are the rollback. Configuration is slot-specific where the environments differ.

Azure Functions covers a short job or an event: a queue message, a timer, an HTTP call that finishes. AKS is for a team that has chosen Kubernetes and will own the cluster upgrades. A single web app is not a reason to start AKS.

Azure SQL, Storage, and Service Bus

Azure SQL is the relational store when the application speaks SQL Server. Blob Storage holds objects. Service Bus carries commands and events that must be retried independently of the web request.

Private endpoints or service endpoints keep that data off the public internet when the subscription supports them. The app identity is the principal on the firewall rule.

Typical use cases

Azure fits teams that already sign in with Entra ID and host on Microsoft services, whether the application is .NET or another runtime App Service can run.

A .NET site on App Service

The application is ASP.NET or a similar web stack. App Service runs it, slots carry the new version, and Azure SQL is reached with a managed identity. The publish profile is not the deployment process.

A timer or a queue worker on Functions

A message arrives on Service Bus or a clock fires. The function does one job, writes its outcome, and can be retried. It does not grow into the web application.

A container platform with an owner

AKS when several services share a cluster and a person is named for upgrades. Workload identity and namespaces are part of the first release. App Service or Container Apps stays the recommendation when that owner does not exist.

Identity already in Entra ID

Employees sign in with the tenant you have. The application uses that tenant for users, and a separate app registration or managed identity for itself. Guest accounts and admin roles are not the same group.

How we work

An Azure engagement names the resource group, the identity, and the host before feature work depends on them.

Place the environment in a resource group

One group per environment, tagged, with a budget alert if you use budgets. Resources that share a lifecycle live together. A shared group for everything is the habit we replace.

Decide App Service, Functions, or AKS

Site or API, short job, or cluster. The choice includes who patches the platform. .NET on App Service is the common path for the applications we already build. Another runtime is fine when the host supports it and the team can run it.

Use Entra ID for users and for the app

Users come from the tenant. The app uses a managed identity toward Azure SQL, Storage, and Service Bus. Local development has a documented way to sign in that does not copy production secrets into a laptop file.

Deploy with the pipeline that exists

Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions builds, tests, and deploys to a slot or a staging resource group. Swapping a slot or rerunning the previous release is practiced before production is the only environment.

Frequently asked questions

Questions about Azure hosting and how it meets the application.

Do you only host .NET on Azure?

No. .NET on App Service is a common path because that is a stack we already build. Node, Python, Java, and containers are in scope when Azure is the right host and the team can operate that runtime. The language pages describe the application. This page describes the platform.

When do you recommend AKS?

When you have several services, a reason to run Kubernetes, and a person who will upgrade the cluster. Otherwise App Service, Functions, or Container Apps is the smaller system. We will recommend the smaller one.

Can you use our Azure DevOps project?

Yes. We add the pipeline steps to the project you have: build, test, deploy to a slot or a staging resource group, then promote. GitHub Actions is the alternative when that is already the CI system. We do not install a third system beside either one.

How should data be reached from the app?

With a managed identity to Azure SQL, Storage, or Service Bus, on a private path when the subscription supports it. Connection strings, if they remain, are secrets in the app configuration, different per slot, and absent from the repository.

What about AWS and Google Cloud?

Both have their own pages. Choose Azure when identity, SQL Server, and the operational habit are already Microsoft. A system can still call a service hosted elsewhere. That call is an API with a timeout, not a shared administrator account.
